subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Tea Polyphenols and Health
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Tea Polyphenols and Health.

hook.text: Tea leaves are packed with polyphenols—compounds that protect cells, reduce inflammation, and fight oxidative stress.

buildup.text: Green tea is richest in catechins, especially EGCG—one of the most studied antioxidants in nutrition science.

discovery.text: EGCG has shown anti-cancer, anti-inflammatory, and cardiovascular benefits in hundreds of laboratory studies.

twist.text: Lab results don't always translate to real life. The body absorbs only 2–5% of ingested EGCG—most gets broken down.

climax.text: Despite low absorption, populations with high green tea intake consistently show lower cancer and heart disease rates.

punchline.text: Small absorption, big population effects. Tea polyphenols add up over a lifetime.

quiz.question: What is EGCG?
options: A catechin antioxidant abundant in green tea with extensive health research

details.summary: Tea is rich in polyphenols, especially catechins in green tea and theaflavins in black tea. These compounds act as antioxidants, reduce inflammation, and have been linked to lower risks of heart disease, certain cancers, and neurodegenerative conditions in large-scale studies.
details.whyItMatters: Tea's health benefits extend far beyond caffeine. Polyphenols give tea a unique health profile that distinguishes it from coffee and other caffeinated beverages.
takeaways: Green tea is rich in catechins; black tea in theaflavins
Polyphenols act as antioxidants and reduce inflammation
Large studies link tea consumption to lower chronic disease risk

faq.question: Which type of tea has the highest concentration of health polyphenols?
faq.answer: Green tea, especially matcha, has the highest catechin content because minimal processing preserves these compounds. White tea also retains high polyphenol levels. Heavily oxidized black teas convert catechins into different beneficial compounds.

faq.question: Does adding milk to tea reduce its polyphenol health benefits?
faq.answer: Some studies suggest milk proteins can bind to catechins and reduce their antioxidant availability. However, the evidence is mixed, and the overall health benefits of tea consumption appear to persist regardless of milk addition.
